stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into soft sediment, they slow down. Their amplitude grows as they slow, so the ground shakes harder. After a moderate earthquake in 2024, seismologist Ines Kovač compared readings from five monitoring stations. She concluded that, among stations the same distance from the epicenter, those built on sediment recorded stronger shaking than those built on bedrock. For example, ______

Peak Ground Acceleration at Five Stations, 2024 Earthquake
Station | Distance from epicenter (km) | Ground type | Peak acceleration (% g)
S1 | 12 | Bedrock | 9
S2 | 12 | Sediment | 21
S3 | 30 | Bedrock | 4
S4 | 30 | Sediment | 11
S5 | 8 | Sediment | 26
choices: Station S5, on sediment 8 km from the epicenter, recorded 26% g, whereas Station S3, on bedrock 30 km away, recorded 4% g.
Station S3, on bedrock 30 km from the epicenter, recorded 4% g, whereas Station S4, on sediment 30 km away, recorded 11% g.
Station S2, on sediment 12 km from the epicenter, recorded 21% g, whereas Station S4, on sediment 30 km away, recorded 11% g.
Station S1, on bedrock 12 km from the epicenter, recorded 21% g, whereas Station S2, on sediment 12 km away, recorded 9% g.
explanation: Kovač's claim is limited to stations the same distance from the epicenter. So you need two stations at one distance, one on each ground type, with the sediment station shaking harder. S3 and S4 are both 30 km away, and S4, on sediment, recorded 11% g against S3's 4% g on bedrock.

A.why: The numbers are right, and sediment does beat bedrock here, but you missed the scope words 'the same distance.' S5 is much closer to the epicenter than S3, so distance could explain the whole gap, and the choice can't show that ground type made the difference.

C.why: This is an accurate reading, but both stations sit on sediment. You are comparing distances when the claim is about ground type, so the choice shows that shaking weakens farther away, which is a different point.

D.why: You swapped the values. S1 on bedrock recorded 9% g and S2 on sediment recorded 21% g, so this choice reverses the direction the table shows.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
In the widely told tale of the stolen fire, the thief is a clever animal whose species varies from place to place. Folklorist Amara Oyelaran catalogued 412 recorded versions of the tale from four regions. She argues that the trickster's form reflects the storytellers' landscape more than their language: even where the same language is spoken, coastal and inland communities favor different tricksters. For instance, ______

Versions of the Stolen-Fire Tale by Region
Region | Language | Setting | Versions with a heron trickster (%)
Varnel | Oskan | Coastal | 72
Dorrow | Oskan | Inland | 18
Pelle | Mirran | Coastal | 69
Istek | Mirran | Inland | 21
choices: 72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 21% of versions from inland Istek.
72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 69% of versions from coastal Pelle.
72% of versions from inland Dorrow feature a heron trickster, compared with 18% of versions from coastal Varnel.
72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 18% of versions from inland Dorrow.
explanation: The example has to show two communities that share a language but differ in setting, with different tricksters. Varnel and Dorrow both speak Oskan. Coastal Varnel uses the heron in 72% of versions and inland Dorrow in only 18%, so landscape, not language, accounts for the difference.

A.why: The figures are correct and the setting differs, but you overlooked 'even where the same language is spoken.' Varnel speaks Oskan and Istek speaks Mirran, so language could explain the gap as well as landscape could.

B.why: This is accurate, but it shows two coastal regions being similar. The sentence has to show coastal and inland communities differing within a single language, and this pair differs in language, not setting.

C.why: You attached each figure to the wrong region. Dorrow is inland with 18% and Varnel is coastal with 72%, so this choice reverses the pattern.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Soluble fiber such as oat beta-glucan forms a gel in the stomach. The gel slows how quickly food reaches the small intestine, and so how fast glucose enters the blood. A research team gave adults with either normal or impaired glucose tolerance a standard breakfast, or the same breakfast with added beta-glucan. The team concluded that the fiber's benefit was not uniform: it blunted the post-meal glucose rise considerably more in adults with impaired tolerance. For example, ______

Average Rise in Blood Glucose After Breakfast (mg/dL)
Group | Standard breakfast | Breakfast with beta-glucan
Normal tolerance | 48 | 41
Impaired tolerance | 92 | 63
choices: the fiber reduced the glucose rise by 29 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance but by only 7 mg/dL in adults with normal tolerance.
the fiber reduced the glucose rise from 92 mg/dL to 63 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance, a drop of nearly one-third.
impaired-tolerance adults eating the fiber breakfast had a larger rise (63 mg/dL) than normal adults eating the standard one (48 mg/dL).
the fiber reduced the glucose rise by 7 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance but by 29 mg/dL in adults with normal tolerance.
explanation: The claim is comparative: the fiber helped one group more than the other. To show that, you need the size of the fiber's effect in both groups. It was 92 − 63 = 29 mg/dL for impaired tolerance and 48 − 41 = 7 mg/dL for normal tolerance, and only this choice puts those two numbers side by side.

B.why: This is accurate, and it does show the fiber working in impaired-tolerance adults. But the claim is that the benefit was larger in that group than in the other, and this choice never mentions the normal-tolerance group, so nothing is compared.

C.why: Both numbers are correct, but you compared people on different breakfasts from different groups. That shows impaired-tolerance adults still have higher spikes, not that the fiber did more for them.

D.why: You attached the reductions to the wrong groups. The 29 mg/dL drop belongs to the impaired-tolerance group, so this choice reverses the finding.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Economists have argued that offering remote work reduces quitting mainly because it spares employees costly commutes. If that explanation is correct, the option should matter little at firms where commutes are already short. Analyzing records from 2,300 mid-sized firms, labor economist Tomás Reyes found that this prediction held: ______

Annual Quit Rates at Mid-Sized Firms
Average commute | Remote option offered | Quit rate (%)
Long | Yes | 11
Long | No | 19
Short | Yes | 12
Short | No | 13
choices: firms with long commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 11%, compared with 19% for long-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 19% for long-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 13% for short-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 19% for short-commute firms that did not.
explanation: The prediction is about short-commute firms only: there, remote work should make little difference. So you need the two short-commute groups, with and without the option. Their quit rates are 12% and 13%, which are nearly the same, and that is exactly what the prediction expects.

A.why: This is a true and striking comparison, but it concerns long-commute firms. The prediction Reyes tested was that the option matters little where commutes are short, and a big effect at long-commute firms doesn't show that.

B.why: The numbers are accurate, but the two firms differ in both commute length and remote policy. A mismatched pair can't isolate what remote work does at short-commute firms.

D.why: You misread the table. Short-commute firms without remote work had a 13% quit rate, not 19%, and the false figure would suggest a large effect, the opposite of what Reyes found.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
In most metals, shrinking the crystal grains raises hardness, because the boundaries between grains block the dislocations that let a metal deform. Materials scientist Hye-jin Park suspected that this effect has a limit. When grains become extremely small, she reasoned, the boundaries themselves begin to slide, and hardness should drop. Testing nickel samples of varying grain size, Park found evidence of such a reversal: ______

Hardness of Nickel Samples by Grain Size
Sample | Average grain size (nm) | Hardness (GPa)
P | 200 | 3.1
Q | 80 | 4.4
R | 35 | 5.6
S | 18 | 6.0
T | 8 | 5.2
choices: the sample with 200 nm grains had a hardness of 3.1 GPa, while the sample with 35 nm grains had a hardness of 5.6 GPa.
the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa, while the sample with 200 nm grains had a hardness of 3.1 GPa.
the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.
the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.
explanation: A reversal means that at the smallest sizes, smaller grains give lower hardness, the opposite of the usual trend. Going from 18 nm to 8 nm, hardness falls from 6.0 GPa to 5.2 GPa. That is the drop Park predicted.

A.why: This is accurate, but it shows the ordinary trend, where smaller grains mean harder metal. The sentence promises evidence of a reversal, and this pair shows the rule working as usual.

B.why: Both figures are correct, but comparing the smallest grains with the largest just shows that 8 nm nickel is harder than 200 nm nickel, which fits the usual trend. The reversal only appears when you compare the two smallest sizes.

C.why: You swapped the hardness values. The 18 nm sample measured 6.0 GPa and the 8 nm sample 5.2 GPa, so this version would make the smallest grains hardest, which is no reversal at all.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Over the past fifty years, a new pronunciation of the vowel in words like "boat" has spread outward from the city of Aldren. Dialect geographers long assumed that such changes move like ripples, reaching nearer towns first. After surveying four towns, linguist Petra Lindqvist concluded that travel links can matter more than sheer distance: a town tied to Aldren by rail may be further along in the change than a town that sits closer but lacks a rail link. For example, ______

Use of the New Vowel in Four Towns
Town | Distance from Aldren (km) | Rail link | Speakers using new vowel (%)
Brisk | 40 | Yes | 57
Coll | 95 | No | 33
Eske | 150 | Yes | 49
Dunmere | 160 | No | 12
choices: 49% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 33% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
49% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 12% in Dunmere, 160 km away without one.
57% of speakers in Brisk, 40 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 33% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
33% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 49% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
explanation: The claim needs a rail town that is farther from Aldren and still further along in the change than a closer town without rail. Eske is 150 km away with rail and has 49%. Coll is only 95 km away without rail and has 33%. The ripple model can't explain that, but rail can.

B.why: This is accurate, and the rail town does lead. But Dunmere is farther from Aldren than Eske, so plain distance could explain Eske's lead. The claim specifically needs the town without rail to be the closer one.

C.why: The numbers are right, but Brisk is both closer to Aldren and on the rail line. Its lead fits the ripple model just as well, so it can't show that rail outweighs distance.

D.why: You swapped the two towns' percentages. Eske has 49% and Coll has 33%, and the reversed figures would make the rail town lag behind.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Many reef fish spend their larval stage in open water, then locate a reef partly by listening for the crackle of snapping shrimp and the calls of resident fish. Marine biologist Kalani Akana tested whether ocean warming interferes with this behavior. She placed clownfish larvae in four tanks, each broadcasting sound recorded at either a healthy or a degraded reef, at one of two temperatures. Akana concluded that warmer water blunts larvae's response to healthy-reef sound. For example, ______

Clownfish Larvae Settlement by Tank
Tank | Recording | Water temperature (°C) | Larvae settled (%)
1 | Healthy reef | 26 | 58
2 | Degraded reef | 26 | 31
3 | Healthy reef | 30 | 34
4 | Degraded reef | 30 | 29
choices: 58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 31% of larvae hearing degraded-reef sound at 26°C.
34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 30°C, compared with 29% of larvae hearing degraded-reef sound at 30°C.
58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound at 30°C.
34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound at 30°C.
explanation: To show that warmth blunts the response to healthy-reef sound, keep the recording the same and change only the temperature. Tanks 1 and 3 both played healthy-reef sound. Settlement fell from 58% at 26°C to 34% at 30°C.

A.why: This is a correct reading, but both tanks were at 26°C. It shows that larvae prefer healthy-reef sound, which is the behavior being studied, not that warming weakens it.

B.why: The figures are accurate, but both tanks were at 30°C. Without a cooler comparison you can't tell from this pair whether warming changed anything.

D.why: You swapped the temperatures. 58% settled at 26°C and 34% at 30°C, and the reversed version would suggest warming strengthens the response.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Plants absorb carbon dioxide through tiny leaf pores called stomata. When atmospheric CO₂ is abundant, a plant can take in enough through fewer pores, so leaves grown in CO₂-rich air tend to have lower stomatal density. After examining fossil ginkgo leaves from rock layers spanning an ancient warming event, paleobotanist Rafael Quintero concluded that CO₂ rose during the event and then returned to earlier levels. For example, ______

Stomatal Density of Fossil Ginkgo Leaves
Layer | Age (million years ago) | Timing | Stomata per mm²
1 | 56.4 | Before event | 142
2 | 56.0 | During event | 88
3 | 55.8 | During event | 91
4 | 55.2 | After event | 137
choices: stomatal density fell from 142 per mm² before the event to 88 per mm² during it, a decline of nearly 40%.
stomatal density fell from 142 per mm² before the event to 88 during it and then rose to 137 afterward.
stomatal density was 88 per mm² in the earlier layer from the event and 91 in the later layer from it.
stomatal density rose from 88 per mm² before the event to 142 during it and then fell to 137 afterward.
explanation: Quintero's conclusion has two parts: CO₂ rose, then came back down. Because density moves opposite to CO₂, you need a drop during the event and a recovery after it. This choice shows both: 142 fell to 88 and then rose to 137.

A.why: This is accurate and supports the first half of the conclusion, that CO₂ rose. But it stops before the event ends, so it says nothing about CO₂ returning to earlier levels.

C.why: Both values are correct, but both come from during the event. Two nearly equal readings from inside the event can't show a rise or a return.

D.why: You misplaced the values. Density was 142 before the event and 88 during it, and the reversed order would suggest CO₂ fell during the warming.
